utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour -- Mr. President and Your Honours. Now doubt you have noticed that the witness who was here resembles in no way the witness who was here when we finished yesterday. I assume you have been informed that the witness who was started yesterday has fallen ill and cannot continued today. We hope that he will be able to continue tomorrow, but in the meantime we have substituted the next witness. Before the witness begins, I did -- because I think I'll only be here during the first session today, we had intended -- we were supposed to report to Your Honours with respect to agreed facts and intercepts, and I believe the Defence would like to address Your Honours about it. And if we could just do it briefly while I'm here, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Firstly, we hope that the witness will recover and will be well enough to continue his testimony tomorrow. But in the event that is he not, I think it's better not to bring him. Just bring him when you're fairly certain that he will be able to continue his evidence to the end. So, Mr. Tapuskovic, you want to address us on agreed facts briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say is that we're going to finalise this within a few days. There's no dispute among us there. I am not going to talk about numbers, but at any rate there are a number of facts that are indisputable which will be presented and submitted in the course of the next few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is meant by "the next few days?" Today is Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, if I could just clarify that that also applies to the intercepts by the end of this week, because that was the other matter that was outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want Mr. Tapuskovic to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If he could, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does that also apply to intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I delegated this issue to my colleague, Ms. Branislava Isailovic, and before the witness enters the courtroom we can state our position immediately. We can do it even today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't understand that. Before the witness? Oh, you mean the intercept witness? I'm not clear as to what was meant. Which witness are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to avoid further confusion, in the same spirit and sense that we said with respect to indisputable facts, we're going to state our position regarding intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, I think that's clear enough now. Yes. Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. Ms. Edgerton, you're going to lead this witness. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. Ms. Edgerton you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If it's of any assistance, I should note that this witness will testify about a sniping incident which took place on March 6th, 1995, which we also refer to as SN 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Tarik Zunic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zunic, I know you understand English quite well, so as we go through the questions today, I'd like to remind you to please wait until the translation into your own language is concluded before answering the question just to make sure that everything is perfectly clear. Could you tell us, are you working at present?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what are you doing?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I'm finishing my studies, university studies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In what area?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: The faculty of transport.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could pull up PT 2901, please. I'll be referring to two documents, 2901 and then 2902. If you could make either of those available on the monitor, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It appears that we're having some problems with the e-court system. If I could ask your indulgence for maybe 10, 15 more seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do have hard copies of the English language versions available to me, Your Honour, and since both of those were signed by the witness, we may be able to proceed with those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We have them. The Chamber has them and I'd be prepared to make at least one available to a party that doesn't have one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I see on the monitor in front of me we have the B/C/S version of 2901 available, so I think we're in fine shape, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zunic, on the screen in front of you, you see a copy of a statement dated 10 November 1995 to officials of the OTP. Did you have an opportunity to review this document prior to your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if the English language version could be given back to the witness, because that's the version he signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on the English document, do you recognise your signature?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And on the English document another signature appears immediately below yours. Who's that?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: That's my mother's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall whether this statement was read back to you in your own language before you and your mother put your signatures to it?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I tender that as the first exhibit for this witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P184, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why is his mother's signature there?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, it's a question best asked of the witness, but I note at the time he was, if my math is accurate, around 14 years of age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let him say so. For the record. Why is your mother's signature there as well as yours? Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to offer an explanation that could be helpful to the Chamber. First of all, I would like to make a correction. The Prosecutor said "around 14 years of age" and I think it's more 15 years of age. According to the laws in force at the time, including in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was a so-called younger minor and under such circumstances a parent must always be present when such a statement is being made. That is what the law prescribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Is that why your mother's signature is there? I still want to hear from the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Could we move next to document 2902, please, an ICTY statement signed by the witness, dated 21 April 2006. If it's of assistance, perhaps he could be given the English language copy of that one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zunic, at different times on the screen in front of you you've seen now the statement of 21 April 2006 in your language and an English translation. Did you have an opportunity to review both those documents prior to testifying today?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was that second statement also read back to you in your own language before signing?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to both these statements, could you tell the Trial Chamber whether you would answer those questions the same way if you were to testify more fully today?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have the second document, 2902, marked as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P185, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to move to a map which bears -- which is already in evidence and bears the number P104, please. I will note for Your Honours that the greater part of Mr. Zunic's time here in court today will be spent dealing with the map and some photographs, some illustrative photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long is he scheduled for?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was a little intimidated by your reference to "the greater part" of his time spent here today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps a bad choice of words, Your Honour. As always, we will try to be as efficient as possible with the time allotted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's 1.5, one and a half hours?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sure we can be very efficient with that time, Your Honours. I see now the map in front of us. If I could have the right-hand part of the map, the eastern part of the map, magnified, please. If you could move the magnification a little further up towards the top of the page, to the north, and a little bit further -- stop. And a little bit to the east, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zunic, do you see the map in front of you on your monitor?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you find your school on this map?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: It has to be moved a little bit to the left, please. Opposite side. Yes, I can see my school.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, using the electronic marking tool that's attached to the monitor on the right, would you be able to mark your school with an X and designate it with the number 1, please.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you see your home on this map, the location of your home, I should said.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you please mark that and designate it with the number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, can you mark the route you took home from school on the day you were shot, please.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Shall I mark the whole route between my home and the school, or just a section thereof?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think it doesn't take any longer for you to mark the whole route. While you're doing that, could you tell us whether you had to walk -- could you describe the walk that you took. Was it uphill, downhill? Was the terrain flat?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: One part of the route as far as Skenderija was flat, and towards the Sedrenik neighbourhood, it was uphill.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you mark where you were shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I note for the record that the route between home and school is the red line joining the numbers 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it possible to enlarge this map a little?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At this moment it would be done with difficulty. Can you mark the approximate area with the number 3, please.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with an arrow, could you mark the direction in which you were walking when you were shot, to make it absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was the front line, to the best of your recollection, visible from the location where you were shot?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: The lines at Spicasta Stijena were visible. These were Serbian positions, whereas the Bosnian positions were not visible.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. If the front line was visible, could you then use an arrow to mark its direction from the location in which you were shot.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could you mark the direction -- the arrow that marks the direction in which you were walking with the number 4, please. That would be the first arrow.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the second arrow denoting the direction of the front line with the number 5, please.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have that marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P186, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the distance of the front line from the place where you were shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say with 100 per cent certainty, but it was between 700 and 900 metres, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move now to a photograph which bears the number 2925, and I will be asking Mr. Zunic to mark that photograph as well, if you could remain there, please, and assist him. My apologies. 2926, please. Your indulgence for a moment. What I see ... Can we, with this photograph, draw further back, please. Your Honours, what seems to have been uploaded in e-court is a zoomed-in version of the photograph I'd intended. However, I do have a hard copy here, and perhaps we could move to the ELMO, in the interests of being expeditious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In essence, it's the same photograph, however, a cropped-off version of the centre, and I think there's an interest, again for the sake of clarity and everyone's understanding, in seeing the neighbourhood at this stage and then moving in somewhat closer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zunic, could you look at the photograph beside you and tell us, does this photo, among other things, depict the location at which you were shot on March 6th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is there anything different between this photo and how you recall the area on that date?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that there are a few new houses that have been built, that the trees have grown over the past 12 years, and that would be it. And another thing, this photograph was taken in summertime and I was wounded at the end of winter.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you mark the location at which you were shot on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And can we somehow move the ELMO up a bit so -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Wonderful. Can you mark the location where you shot on this photograph with an X and denote it with the number 1. You may need another marker.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is your family home depicted on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you also mark that, perhaps with the number 2.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with an arrow, could you mark the direction in which you were walking at the time you were shot and denote it with the number 3.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With an arrow, can you mark the direction of the front line.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can't see anything on the photographs. There are no markings there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the first number 3 is not very clear. Maybe he could remark that. Have you pushed the ELMO button? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you mark with the number 4 the arrow that you've just used to designate the direction of the front line.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were there any houses or other obstructions between that spot, number 1, at which you were shot, and the area leading up to the front line, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were no houses or other structures between me and the front line while I was standing at the place where I was shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember during 1994 and 1995 seeing any Bosnian military positions in locations around your home?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Nowhere in the vicinity were there any positions of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you ever recall seeing or hearing any Bosnian army or military troop movements up to the front line past your house?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I heard, but I didn't see that there were troop movements mainly by night but very rarely in day-time, almost never, because the army avoided movements during day-time in order to avoid putting civilians at risk.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have this photograph, that hard copy, marked as the next exhibit, please. And I'll move on to 2926, which is available electronically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let that be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P187, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, let's have the picture back on the screen, on the ELMO. Mr. Witness, when Judge Robinson asked you how far was the front line from the location where you were, you said approximately 700 metres. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 700 to 900, but I'm not sure because, in fact, I never saw it and I never read anything precise about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. This front line, what does it mean precisely? There was the ABiH and then on the opposite side, the army of the Republika Srpska. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I didn't hear your answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. How far, approximately, was the ABiH and the army of the Republika Srpska from the place where the incident took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you perhaps put it more clearly, because I really didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here's my question again: There's a front line. There are two different warring factions. If there's an army that's 700 metres away from the place where you were wounded, it means that the other army, which is in the opposite side, is also at some distance from you. What was that distance? Because we have two different armies on the front line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no way I can know it. I have never been on that front line, nor have I ever seen it during the war. I only saw it much later when I went to see those positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one question arising from this latest answer, Mr. Zunic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said that you have seen these positions much later. Do I take it from that that you've, since the war, been to the location of the former front line?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I only went to Spicasta Stijena because the rest was still full of mines, and that area of Spicasta Stijena was cleared so you could go there. I didn't see the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your estimate of 700 to 900 metres, then, is based, to a certain extent, on your having visited that location since the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: On that basis, but also on the basis of stories I heard from others, from other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could move now to the photograph 29 -- perfect, thank you. Is that 2925 or 2926? 2926. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zunic, on this photograph, are you able to see the location at which you were shot with some greater clarity than in the previous photograph?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I can see the place. It's almost the same. There's no great difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again, could you mark it. With the number 1 as well, please.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And can you mark again the direction from which the shots which hit you were fired.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With the number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now, again, to make things perfectly clear, as you were walking, on which side of you did the front line lay?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: You mean which side was I facing?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Which side of you did the front line lay on? Where did it sit in relation to your position?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: It was to my left.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have this photograph marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, is the Prosecution going to bring evidence as to how the front line was constituted, where the Serb position was and where the ABiH position was? For example, in relation to this incident, it would be important to know where the ABiH position was at the time when this witness was shot. He doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. He doesn't know, quite so, and yes, that is our intention. We will be calling that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could move on now to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's a bit confusing, because the witness also said that the positions were not visible from that point. So I'm just waiting for your leading him to answering the question of whether he knew where the positions were but just could not see them or whether he didn't know where they were at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could go back to the transcript, Your Honours, it's my recollection that the witness said the Bosnian army positions were not visible from that point; however, he was able to see the Serb army positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. But that would imply that he knew where the Bosnian positions were but he just couldn't see them from there, and there's a different.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and we will get there at the time of the next exhibit, which is PT 2716. It's a further photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see this photograph on the screen in front of you, Mr. Zunic?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I see the same picture as before.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies. We'll be playing this photograph from here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see a new picture on your screen, Mr. Zunic?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: On the other screen, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, does the marking of the lower part of this photograph accurately reflect the location at which you were shot on March 6, 1995?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Do you see a new photograph on the picture in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at the previous photograph, the position where he was standing was not drawn in, although the Prosecutor asked the witness to mark it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to make the same point, because the -- you have presented a photograph with a position marked, already marked, and you have asked the witness whether that marked position represents the area where he was shot. It is the witness who should give the evidence as to where he was shot and then you mark the position, unless some evidence was led previously that the area marked is equivalent to the area in relation to which he has already testified as being the place where he was shot. Otherwise, it's very leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could move back, then, to the photograph immediately prior to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, generally, I should say that I will not allow markings which are not made by the witness to be put to the witness as markings relating to his incident. The evidence must emanate from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What I propose to do, then, Your Honour, is skip over this photograph entirely and move on to the next one. I think that might be more expeditious and take us to the point here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zunic, can you look at the photograph in front of you and tell us whether this reflects the location at which you were shot on March 6, 1995.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, with a margin of error of a metre or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is there anything different between this photo and how recall the area 12 years ago?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The houses have been renovated. The trees are green and they have grown over the past 12 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let him show the place where he was standing when he was shot on this photograph and let him mark it. Because on the previous photograph, he showed us that he was standing in a field. Let him show on this photo whether he was standing in a field or on the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, where were you standing when you were shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I first say that I wasn't standing at all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as this gentleman suggests. I was moving, and at that point I was in the spot marked by 1; not in the valley, not on a surface covered with grass, but on this street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let him show that spot on that photograph, the place where he was standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please show us that spot where you were, where you were moving, not standing. You were walking, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Keeping in mind, Your Honour, that this is the beginning of the 360-degree panoramic photograph which has been the subject, I understand, of much discussion in this courtroom already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but all these matters are matters of contention and so the witness is not to be led to evidence relating to it. On the photograph that we have on the screen, can you indicate where you were? If not, then we can move the photograph, because, it is, as you said, a photograph of 360 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I've not made myself totally clear. , this being the 360, is not a photograph he can mark. However, the previous two obviously were. If there's a need, I can have a series of still photographs made very quickly so that they can be marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what can he say about this photograph? If he can't mark it, let him -- Can you say in words anything that is relevant to your incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a new photograph showing this little shop and the fence. That's where I was, a metre forward or backwards, but that is with 100 per cent certainty the spot where I was as I was moving towards my home. That's where I was when I was shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little more specifically where on the photograph? Because I see the shop and I see a fence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of this fence, the front of the picture, to the right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What's your point?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want him to mark that spot where he says he was standing on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not technically possible. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. And I would have thought the two -- the markings on the two previous photographs might have obviated the need at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you will, of course, be cross-examining and you can raise this point. But from what I understand, you can have a still made which could be marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that wouldn't take very long?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd have to make some inquiries, but I would hope to have it -- I would hope to have it in the next session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will require that, that you produce the still.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And at the time we take the break later on this morning, Your Honour, I think we can achieve that. We may ask for five minutes longer to be able to make the copies. Of course, they won't be electronically uploaded, but we'll have copies available for Your Honours and for the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What I propose to do, then, Your Honour, is to leave this portion of my questioning with respect to this panoramic photograph until after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I can only observe that the witness was scheduled for an hour and a half on both sides, I think. Let's proceed. Let's proceed, because you have already demonstrated the place where he was shot. If it can be produced, then let it be produced. But we shouldn't waste time. It may be that the photograph will have to be evaluated by the Chamber in light of the evidence presented.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. I misunderstood Your Honours. I understood that I was to produce a photograph for the witness to mark. At this point we will continue with the examination-in-chief for the comments of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you've already indicated a number of times that this does reflect the location at which you were shot in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask that this photograph be rotated to the right, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us, as we move through the photograph, if you see the location which you've marked on the previous photographs, 188 and 187, as being the direction from which the shot which hit you was fired.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Right there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, when you say "Right there" --

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: No, I meant to say stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you describe to us what you see on the photograph at this moment.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately beyond that second pillar supporting the fence, you can see the top, the peak, of the Spicasta Stijena from where the shot came.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've described earlier that the front line was visible from the location at which you were shot?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you see that location, what you believe to have been the front line depicted on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: From here you can only see the Serb positions that were on Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Based on your later visits to the front lines and your observations from this day, are you able to offer any guidance as to where the Bosnian positions were in relation to the Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I could, but only roughly. I could not do it with 100 per cent certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Which positions lay closer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask, in order to facilitate cross-examination, to make another freeze from this photograph regarding this point so that the witness could show the positions briefly, to make another freeze which the witness could mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us see where the Prosecutor is going and then we'll decide on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zunic, you indicated that since the war you have been to the front line, the former front line.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I said I only went to Spicasta Stijena because the other areas are full of mines. It's dangerous to walk there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Based on your observations, which faction lay closer to the location at which you were shot?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Which of the two warring factions was closer to the location at which you were shot?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was closer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Based on your observations, do you have any idea why Bosnian army positions weren't visible at the time you were shot?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Because they were at the very foot of Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then in relation to them, based on your observations, where were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it observations or what he was told? When did he go there? When did you go to the front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And were the front lines there then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can see some remnants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you go by yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, with friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How were you able to determine where the front lines was? Just by observation or was it based on what you were told, or maybe by both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I walked all the way up to the line previously held by the Serb army where you can see the bunkers, the trenches, and all of their positions that are now within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And to add on to what His Honour has been asking you, at the time of the incident, at the time you were shot, did you have any knowledge of where the front lines were; and, if so, what was the source of that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: The first thing, you could hear on the radio that people were telling; plus I could see it with my own eyes every day as I was walking.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours have further questions at this moment, I propose to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zunic, can we talk about the jacket you were wearing at the time that you were shot, which you describe in your statements as green.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. It was not an olive-drab green. It was just a normal green, let's say, Benetton green.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were you carrying anything at the time?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a blue rucksack with my school books and other things on my right shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask you right now to stand up and show the Court how you were carrying the rucksack at the time you were shot.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I carried it over my right shoulder and I was holding it with my right hand. Is this all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And now if you could just indicate, where, in relation to you, was the front line?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I was moving in this direction and the front line was to my left.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Take your seat again, please. Now, I note the information in both your statements that you were hit in the right hand; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was hit in the right hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you also describe bullet-holes in the left front part of your jacket at heart level, and I wonder if you could explain for the Trial Chamber how this happened.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: That happened while I was walking and carrying my rucksack on my right shoulder. The bullets that came from Spicasta Stijena first entered the left part of my jacket, exited through the right-hand side of my jacket, then hit my hand and then exited my hand. I was lucky to have walked not so fast; otherwise, I would have been dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we move to a document on the monitor, please. It bears the number 00150, and it's available in two languages, B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zunic, on the right-hand side of the screen in front of you, do you recognise the document that you see?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the findings following my admission to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could I ask you to just read in your language the sentence that begins with the word "Ranjen ..."

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask for this to be a little bit enlarged. Thank you very much. "Civilian wounded by a sniper bullet in Sedrenik. Perforating wound. Entry point in distal part of right underarm from the radial side; exit point in the thenar area. Status show no abnormalities." Do I have to continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if we can have that marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want to have the witness clarify something. In answer to counsel, you said that the BiH army was nearer to you, to the place where you were shot, than the Serb army, but the BiH army wasn't visible. In terms of the topography, can you explain why, although being nearer, the BiH army wasn't visible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honours. First of all, it was only logical for our army to be closer to us than the Serbian forces. Secondly, Spicasta Stijena is almost vertical with respect to this plateau where our army was and with respect to the whole topography of this area. Therefore, they were on a higher ground and they could be visible with respect to our army. And they also had a very good view of the whole neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the Serb army was on higher ground than the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And between the BiH army and the place where you were shot, what was the topography like which made the BiH army not visible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That ground that reached as far as the BH positions looked like a mild plateau with some lower parts, all the way up to Spicasta Stijena. So there was a very mild ascent moving towards Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zunic, after you were hit and laid down on the ground and until you were rescued, do you recall whether or not there was any further gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Of course I remember. They kept shooting. And they didn't allow me to escape because they knew that they had shot me and that I was lying there, and they kept shooting. I could hear the bullets and the shots being fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you could hear the bullets and the shots being fired, do you remember whether those were single shots or bursts of fire?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Both. That's what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zunic, have you lived in that area the whole war?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was this the first time you had been shot at?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't the first time. It happened, I think, on two occasions that I had been fired on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall having been fired on from any other direction than what you noted as being the front line?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember, actually. They shot at us, myself included, from Spicasta Stijena only.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have any further questions of Mr. Zunic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. As soon as you get the -- as soon as you have the still, let us know. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will exercise due care of the fact that the period when this incident happened that this witness is testifying to now as an adult, but I will have to point out to him a large number of facts relating to this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to avoid any lengthy introductions, Mr. Witness, I know that at the time you were a very young man. My name is Branislav Tapuskovic, an attorney-at-law from Belgrade, and I have to ask you about all these things that you have been telling us today. I will do my best to pose direct questions, and whenever possible I would appreciate if you can answer me with either a yes or no. My first question is as follows: When the war broke out, you were 11 or 12 years old, and when you were shot and wounded, as you described, and given that I know the year in which you were born, you were 14 years and 6 months old. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me read now from the Prosecution exhibit already entered as such - and I also will intended to tender it as a Defence exhibit, which is now not necessary any longer - that is, your statement of the 10th of November which you gave in the presence of your mother. Let me draw your attention to what you said in this statement and then what you said in the statement dated the 21st of April, 2006, when you were already an adult, which is Prosecution Exhibit P185. With regard to the 65 ter document entered as 00150, but as Prosecution Exhibit P18, which refers to this medical paper, and in the bundle of these documents there are two more under 65 ter numbers 02924. Can you confirm this for me, that the first statement that you made you had given at the security office without the presence of your mother?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the statement given on the 11th of March, 1995, which is five days after I had been shot?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember having this conversation?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember, but it's probably the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will remind you of that, then. Let me start with one detail that you mentioned on the 10th of November, in the presence of your mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can pull this up on the screens. That's Prosecution Exhibit 184, page 1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is actually page 2, because page 1 are your personal details. So page 2. Your Honours, please deduct time from my allocated time because I made a mistake. What I wanted to present to the witness was P185, page 2. That's his statement given on the 21st of April, 2006, as an adult man. And if we can have this on our screens, please. Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see your statement that you gave in April 2006? And if you can look at paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read the second passage to you. "The high school that I was attending in 1995 was located in the Pofalici area of Sarajevo. It was a regular school building, and it took about 45 minutes to an hour to walk it." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we have on the screen the photograph P187 which shows the city map. Prosecution Exhibit P187 with the markings of his route to and from school.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think that's properly P104.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P187 is actually the hard copy that was marked by the witness on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. P187 is the photograph. The unmarked city map is P104, and P186 is the marked city mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, can we have the photograph that the witness has marked, where he indicated the route that he took, as he explained to the Prosecutor. Well, this is, again, detrimental to my case and let this time be deduced from my allocated time. Do we have this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you confirmed a minute ago, and you said in 2006, that you had attended secondary school in 1995 in Pofalici, can you please draw a line from your place of residence, a straight line without any curves, to Pofalici. Can you do that for me, as you did here.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: You mean as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Can you imagine it yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I am not going to imagine it.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to draw the line from my school -- from my home to Pofalici?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Witness, you must observe a pause between question and answer - Mr. Tapuskovic knows this - for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I'll pay attention in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me not waste time on this. I wanted something else. What's important is that the witness said that the school is in Pofalici. Now at this point it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you something now about your statement that you remember you gave at the security services centre in Sarajevo on the 11th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 65 ter 02924, dated the 11th of March, 1995. It has been translated. And may I kindly ask for this document to be placed on the screen. 09 -- in fact, 02924, dated the 11th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see that document?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Official Note, dated 11 March 1995; can you see it?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can we have that document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3. Page 3 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: No, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We see the English version on the screen but not the B/C/S one.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem with the system, but the Prosecutor has a hard copy, so that can be placed on the ELMO, the well-tried and ancient procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see it now? I'm not going to read all of it, but I'll read the last paragraph. If the Court wishes me to do so, I can read all of it. But the inspector received the following statement from you five days after the event: "On 6 March 1995, at around 1300 hours, I was returning home from school and I was in Rogina Street. When I same to Sedrenik Street, I heard a gunshot fired from the aggressor's positions at Spicasta Stijena, followed by a sharp pain in my right hand where I sustained an entry and exit wound. I immediately ran for cover and lay down on the ground calling for help. Soon after, members of the UNPROFOR came up to me." Is that the statement you gave five days after the tragedy?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: It may be, but I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to show you another document, which has the 65 ter number 02924, of the 11th of March, 1995, which is before the statement I've just quoted from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that there is an English translation. I need page 3. And if we have the same problem with the system, maybe the Prosecution can show the witness that document. Since it's not on the screen, can I please ask the Prosecution to give him that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see it, Mr. Zunic? Do you see that this document is dated the 10th of March, 1995, taken in the security services? And it says: "On 6 March 1995, this service was informed that in Sedrenik Street, close to the supermarket, a bullet fired from the aggressor's position wounded Tarik Zunic." Is that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: It's not the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not yours. You didn't say it. But this is what I want to ask --

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Bilal Sulejman, an officer from the genocide department, was informed about this. But what matters is this: From the aggressor's position, Tarik Zunic was hit but we could not go to the spot. Instead, we went to the clinical sector where the doctor on duty at the orthopaedic ward, we found out that the wounds sustained were lighter in the area of the right hand. It is, in fact, an entry and exit wound through the hand." Was it really an entry and exit wound in the hand?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes. The bullet came into the palm of my hand and came out in the area of my wrist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My other question is that there are conflicting descriptions; one is that there was heavy gun-fire at Spicasta Stijena and another report says there was just an individual shot.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: As I was walking back, there was gun-fire when I set out, but when I decided, as a 14-year-old, that there was a lull, I thought that there would be -- that it was less dangerous to go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I hear a great deal of overlap between Mr. Zunic and Mr. Tapuskovic, and I have some concern with respect to the English translation in that case. I wonder if they could be reminded to leave a space between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. May I remind you again to observe a pause between question and answer. It's natural, since you're speaking the same language, to overlap, but you have to observe the pause so that the interpreter can be accurate in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just want to finish with the medical document and then it's time for the break. It's P189; it's a medical document. It's the same document that you just had a look at, the medical one. The medical document. Yes, right, that's it. That is the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed it to you a moment ago. It says, from the spot where the Prosecutor asked you to start reading: "Wounded by a sniper bullet in Sedrenik Street as a civilian. Entry and exit wound. Entry point in the distal part of the right lower arm from the radial side." My question is, why did you, as a child, need to be specifically described as a civilian, since you were 14 years old? Why was it necessary to stress that you were a civilian? How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, how is he to say why some officer described him in a particular manner?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, for everybody's information, copies -- still photographs representing every line of view in the 360 panorama that we had been dealing with earlier have been made and distributed. And I should note, they appear in sequence, if one was moving to the right, clockwise, in the photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- or in the panoramic video, and that's the sequence of them. And I have been reminded that I failed to have the panorama -- to request the panorama be marked as an exhibit during my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P190, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may, you may note two photographs rather similar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- of the wooded area. They are not identical photographs, just perhaps indicating 1 or 2 metres difference, to try and give Your Honours and my friends the clearest idea of the topography possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Tapuskovic, you may, of course, utilise the stills in your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With your leave, I would like the registrar to admit as Defence exhibits those two documents, 02924, Official Notes from the 10th of March, 1995, and the 11th of March, 1995. The number I quoted was a 65 ter number, and these Official Notes were made by the security service of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, they are admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 02924 will become Defence Exhibit D43, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Honourable Judge Robinson, you are quite right. The question I just asked before the break is a question better addressed to the doctor that I know will be coming to testify. But there is a question I can ask the witness based on this medical document, and that is the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zunic, you have seen this document and it says that this is an entry and exit wound, whose entry point is in the distal part of the right lower arm, on the radial side. Can you show us where that spot is, according to you, because this is different from what you said before. You said you were shot through the palm of your hand. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I continue to assert that I was shot in the palm of my hand, and I can show it to you, but I do not understand the Latin terms in the medical report and that's not something I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where the radial side is, but I know what the right lower arm is. The medical document says you were hit in the right lower arm, in our Bosnian/Serb, whatever you want to call it, language. How can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I didn't write that; the doctor did. And I still have the scar which shows exactly where I was shot. You can see the entry and the exit points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now ask for the 65 ter number 2901 to be shown. It's a document tendered by the Prosecutor under number 184. It's a statement dated the 10th of November, 1995. Can we see it on the screen. And I will try to be as brief as possible and ask just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is page 1, Mr. Tarik. Can we see page 2. Can I ask you, since this document is now before you, the sixth paragraph begins with the words "I believe ..." Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will read it to you. "I believe that the shots were fired from Spicasta Stijena because it is only from there that the snipers can reach targets in the street." So my question is: You said "I believe" in this statement, which seems to indicate you were not sure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I still believe today that the shots were fired from Spicasta Stijena because it was not possible for the shots to come from any other side. And, anyway, the snipers fired all the time from that direction, from Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But let us read on, and I'm quoting you: "They can reach targets in the street." Do you assert here that only from Spicasta Stijena can shots reach the spot where you were? Can there be no further spot that can reach that target?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You continued to say: "It's possible also to fire at Trebevic, an area held by the Serbs but not with small-calibre weapons. Only anti-aircraft guns can efficiently fire from Trebevic." My question is: Can we, if we read this, conclude that from Trebevic it's not possible to fire with small-calibre weapons?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: You can fire from anything you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us not overlap.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: We are not overlapping. You can fire from wherever you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you said it's possible to fire at targets in the street also from Trebevic, an area held by the Serbs, but not from small-calibre weapons. I'm asking you if what you said is correct.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I can say it is correct because I heard it from grown-ups who knew more about weapons. And as for the area where I was hit, it was not visible from Trebevic. It is clearly stated that the street where I was hit is visible from Trebevic, at least a part of it. What is written here reflects exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But not by a sniper, by guns.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: But not efficiently. That's what people said in view of the distance and the range and the visibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So from that sniping rocket, it was not possible to have a range all the way up to the town.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: The range was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking of the bullet that hit you, you said here in paragraph 5, and is this correct: "I immediately recognised that the shots were fired from the M-84 machine-gun. The sound is distinct from the sound of ordinary guns. I can easily make the difference because I heard so many shots." Now I'm asking you, you know very well what this automatic rifle, M-84, is. Do you know what it is?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I don't know what that automatic rifle is. I've never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand, but you said here that as soon as you heard the shots, you recognised them as coming from an automatic rifle, M-84.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I lived there. I survived. I listened to people older than me all the time. It was on the radio all the time. There were so-called sowers of death. And the automatic rifle is M-84 and I was able to distinguish between the sounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Four paragraphs later on: "While I was there, I discovered that I had two bullet-holes on the front side of my jacket at the level of my heart. I suppose that the bullet made those holes when it passed through my jacket." My question is: In the first days you claimed that you were hit by only one bullet. How come you are now speaking of several bullets?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I still continue to say that only one bullet hit me, and this is an error and I told them it was an error. They told me, the people who drafted this, that it was not important and it would be corrected later. But I see you have picked on this. There were two bullet-holes, one entry on the left side and another exit hole on the right side of my jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And it continued through your hand?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, through the palm of my hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you: Can it be said that you were wearing a vest at the time protecting your chest and the body from bullets that can immediately kill? Can we say that you had a vest that you received in order to protect your life?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I don't know how you came up with that. I never had that vest, nor did I ever wear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to suggest this, because you know very well -- you knew very well at the time what an automatic rifle M-84 is, and from all you say here I have to conclude that you may have also taken part in defending your country from the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Concerning the M-84 automatic rifle, I knew about it from stories of others, from the radio, from the sounds I heard myself. And I was not involved in the army because I was too young, and it never crossed my mind to take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in that territory, between the spot where you were hit and where that ridge of the rock is, were the positions divided in such a way that in one set of the trenches there were troops of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in another set of trenches, on higher ground, there were troops of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking, and that's only normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From these positions, from these trenches, when you finally went to see the location ten years later, what was the distance between these trenches?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: They were divided only by Spicasta Stijena at this particular point, because the Serbian positions were on the top and the Bosnian positions were at the foot of Spicasta Stijena. I still cannot tell you what the difference is. I never measured it, nor have I ever read any relevant data.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You couldn't pass on the other side because of the minefields, but on this side there were no minefields, in order to prevent BiH army soldiers from being killed. You managed somehow to reach that location later on. What is the difference between these positions in metres?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I went to those positions at Spicasta Stijena from the side that, during the war, was held by the Serbs, which means from down, upwards. There were no mines because, of course, nobody in their right mind would plant mines in their area. I didn't climb Spicasta Stijena from the BH army side because it is nearly impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That makes sense. But I'm asking you the distance in metres.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you again, I don't know. I never measured it, nor have I ever read anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In peacetime, on the other side of Stijena, who used to live? Did you have any friends on the other side of Stijena, your peers with whom you played football, who were just living behind the rock?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: You mean the part held by the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And there were people who had been living there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were these people also defending themselves? Did these people on the other side remain in trenches in order to protect their own lives?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just wondering at this point where this is going and how the witness can possibly be expected to comment on what people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, there is merit in that. Move on to another area, Mr. Tapuskovic. This is not getting us anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have, hopefully, enough time to tackle this again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you, when you visited these positions many years later that had been held --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could the transcript please attribute my last statement to me. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From the positions that you saw many years later that had been held by the BH army also had a commanding view of the whole of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I have to repeat it again: I never visited the positions of BH army. I only visited the positions -- Serb-held positions at Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I understand. But from the place where you were hit and from the place where your house was, were you not on the hill that overlooks the whole of Sarajevo; Sedrenik, in other words?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: My house, you cannot see the town at all from my house. Sedrenik, of course, has a good view of the whole of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. From your second statement, I'm going to focus on a few things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2902, a statement given on the 21st of April, 2006. Just a couple of things. So let us start from page 2. Prosecution Exhibit 185, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the beginning?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the page is there. This is page 1. Please take a look at paragraph 4 from the top. Let's skip some other things. It begins "Before ..." Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here you say as follows: "Before the UN arrived, some people tried to help me but one of them was hit. I don't know whether he was killed or wounded at that time, but I know that he eventually died." Can you explain how come that which you hadn't mentioned ever before but only in 2006, to be precise on the 21st of April, you are now saying that there was a man who was killed next to you? First, can you tell me, is this true, what you say here?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: What I say here is true, but I didn't say that he was killed. I said that I didn't know whether he was wounded or killed, but later in my conversations with my parents I heard that this men died many years later of natural causes. I think that's a sufficient explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, it is sufficient, but I have to be very careful how to address you, but I have to ask you directly. So when were you telling the truth, on the first day, on the fifth day after the incident, or ten years later? So how come you are making these kinds of claims here? Is it fair to say that you made this up?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: What I said on the first day and ten years later and what I'm saying now, I'm telling the truth. This information can be checked with the family of this man. When I made the first statement, nobody asked me, and you can see that it contains fewer details than the later one. But when I made my second statement, the investigator was much more thorough and asked me more questions, which you can see from the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So one can deduce that you spoke the truth only in 2006, the truth in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tapuskovic, I don't believe that is a fair question, because the witness has explained that he was not asked in 1995 about that incident, and he even went on to say that the investigator in 2006 was more thorough in the questions put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am convinced that it is true that more people even had been killed. I may suggest that even though he was a young men, he was in a trench as well. But I wanted to ask him something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you that you were in trenches as well.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: You are entitled to do that, absolutely, but this is absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But what I insist on is that you maintained all the time here in this chamber that you heard only one bullet being fired. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: In my first statement, that's what it says, and I read it. That's what I said because I was still under the influence and in shock. And I maintain that shooting was still going on. Some people were trying to help me. And only after an APC came to pick me up and take me to the hospital did the shooting stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before I show you a few photographs, let me ask you this: On your way to school every day -- in the last paragraph on this page, you say: "In the part of the town where I lived, there were no trenches or military installations or barracks." So you still maintain that, in spite of what we heard earlier from you, there were no trenches, no guns or things of that nature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
