utterances.text: Of course, there were trenches on the front line, because I was relatively close to the front line. If you deem this to be incorrect, then let it be so. But I was referring to the proper neighbourhood where we lived. There were no military installations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On your way to school in 1995, did you take this route often? And was there less shooting at that time and that is why you were able to attend school? Is it fair to say that?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't put it like that. There was shooting, but sometimes there were some lulls in order to induce the civilians to get relaxed so that they can target us again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On this 45-minute walk or one-hour walk along the front line, did you ever see any guns, weaponry, tanks, or any other heavy weaponry or mortars, or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think there's ever been any evidence today about this walk to and from school being along the front line, as mentioned here on page 48, lines 20 to 23. I don't think that characterises the evidence properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have to agree, Mr. Tapuskovic. It doesn't reflect the evidence. So the question, then, would be, on this 45-minute walk or one-hour walk, did you ever see any guns, weaponry, tanks or any other heavy weaponry or mortars? What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is, on my way to school, other people moved, not only students, and there was no weaponry or military installations at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So we may deduce that military installations were only on hilltops, or not?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you where the military installations were. I truly don't know. And as for hilltops, I also don't know. I know that they were held by the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the photograph entered as P188 from 65 ter number 02926.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this photograph?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have it enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You marked the place where you were standing at the moment when you were shot.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I was moving towards my house. I'm telling you again, I wasn't standing. I was shot while I was walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, yes, that's what you said. That's correct. But when the Prosecutor showed this photograph to you, you indicated the place where you were shot; is that true?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If that is true, then you were not at all on the street but you were in the field in front of these trees, because if you had been behind the trees you would not have been hit by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you can see where this X is, or are you just looking at this line to the left from X that touches upon this field? But X is precisely on the street. And on top of that, this picture was taken 12 years later and everyone knows that all these trees have grown within these 12 years. In addition to that, it was March, when there were no leaves on the branches, and everyone knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I have never mentioned leaves. You indicated the place where you were standing. It's not in the street; it's in the field. And you just confirmed that it's true. I'm asking you again: Were you in the street or in the field? I'm not interested in trees at all.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I was on the street, as I said earlier, and this X signifies precisely that this is a street, not a field.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A few seconds ago you said that you were at this place and you never showed me the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, Your Honours, I don't wish to waste any more time. We have the photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The difficulty is the X is very big. Perhaps if he had been asked to simply pinpoint just with a dot. But the X, as it is on the photograph, covers both the road, the street, as well as a little of the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is in front of the trees at any rate. In any case, it's in front of the trees, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have his evidence and we have to make of it what we will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In order to save time, I will leave this subject and this photograph. It would be a useless waste of time after everything we have heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to put it again to you. I'm sorry that as a young person, a young man of 15 years of age, you found yourself in the situation with all the rest of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I'm putting it again to you that, as young as you were, you were a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you answer this question for me?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: You are just putting it to me. And second, I am saying again, and there is verifiable, I was not a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. In light of the series of questions with respect to the location at which the witness was standing on page 50, page 51; about the elevations, page 45, line 20, pages 40, 41, and 43, I would to ask that these series of photographs be put before the witness so that we can see them on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In that sequence, please, because it's the sequence that all the parties have received the photographs in. No. Could we just have that first photograph back, please. Yes, that one that is in your hand, if you could place that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zunic, does this photograph depict the location at which you were standing at the time you were shot in March of 1995?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was moving there, and I was hit in the spot which I showed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could you mark that location, if you see it, on this photograph, keeping in mind the comments you have heard now about the size of the markings, please.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I can show it approximately here. It was here. That's where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's the location -- the location you're marking with an X now is the location where you were standing, or where you were moving, as you have corrected me, at the time you were shot. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have that marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Is he also going to show us the direction from which the shots came?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's my intention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P191, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, from P191, if we could move to P1 -- sorry, to the next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zunic, as you were walking, do you see on this photograph what lay to your right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. That's the house that was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know who lived in that house?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They were my parents' family friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have that marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P191, Your Honours. I'm sorry, Your Honours. Registrar's correction: That will be Exhibit P192.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just ask counsel, what is the probative value of this last picture?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I could ask the question now, Your Honours. If Your Honours would indulge me, I would like to go through the photographs and the question will become clearer at the end, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move to the next photograph. I don't think there's a need for that one. The following photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zunic, does this photograph depict the road you were moving along at the time you were shot?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see the location at which you were at the time you were shot?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately here, or maybe lower down the street, as I showed on the first picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again, could you place an X at that location.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately here, or maybe, as in the first picture, a bit lower down.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could you mark with an arrow the direction in which you were moving along the street at the time you were shot, please.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could have that marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P193, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zunic, what do you see on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: I see Spicasta Stijena, or, rather, a part thereof, from which I was hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And as you were moving along the street, to which side of you was this location?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: To my left side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you put an arrow on this photograph, please, indicating the direction of fire.

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the location which you've indicated that the fire is coming from, is that at a higher, lower, or the same elevation as the one at which you were standing?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: It was much higher than the spot where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zunic, how can you be absolutely sure, if you can, that the fire came from this direction and no other?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I can be sure because we were shot at all the time from Spicasta Stijena; second, because of the specific features of my wound, the entry and exit point; and third, because to my right-hand side there was a house that you could see on the previous picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could have P192 put back on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, is this the house that you've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And why do you say that that's the reason that -- one of the reasons that you could only have been shot from the direction of fire that you've indicated?

utterances.speaker: TARIK ZUNIC
utterances.text: Well, because, first of all, they fired all the time from up there; and second, because this house was inhabited by people who were close to me and we were practically one family with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions in re-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. Could I just ask you, in relation to this last piece of evidence that you brought forward, the picture of the house, P192, I understood your question as to imply that perhaps there were bullet-holes in the walls that would confirm that this is where the shots came from. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, that may have been the implication of my question, Your Honour. The witness's response indicates that, given that the house was inhabited by friends of his family, he doesn't believe that any fire could have come from that location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Zunic, that constitutes your evidence. Thank you for giving it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With your permission, I'll take my leave now, Your Honours, and turn the floor over to Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Your next witness, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution calls David Fraser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the time allocated for Mr. Fraser?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The time allocated for Mr. Fraser.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that I will use the balance of this session and all of the following one in my examination-in-chief of this witness, so let's say one and one-half sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Could you begin by telling us your name, your rank, and the armed service of which you are a member.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I am Brigadier General David Fraser. I'm with the Canadian forces, in the army, and I am an infantry officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General Fraser, what is that you currently do in the Canadian army?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I've just finished commanding Regional Command South as part of the multi-national brigade in Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How long have you been in the Canadian army?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I joined the Canadian forces in 1975 as a reserve soldier and then transferred into the regular force in 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to get a summary of some of the experiences you've had in your military career that may be relevant to the testimony I anticipate you will be giving today. Could you summarise for Their Honours the experience you have had in infantry. And I know you said you were an infantry officer.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I have commanded at every rank level, lieutenant, captain, major, lieutenant colonel, and brigadier general, in operations abroad in Cyprus, in Bosnia a couple of times, and in Afghanistan in my trade as an infantry officer, and most recently as an general for a brigade of some 8.000 troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can you summarise for Their Honours your experience with mortars?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: As part of my experience, I have commanded a mortar platoon twice in my career; and also, as a battalion commander, I had mortars working for me; and also as a brigade commander, I had not only mortars but artillery, air, aviation, all supporting operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you please summarise for Their Honours the experience you have had commanding formations that contained snipers?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: As a battalion commander in operations in Bosnia and also, most recently, as a brigade commander, I had snipers working for me and I have employed them, as I said, in operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And lastly, you mentioned that you have had command overseas. Is that co-extensive with your experience with the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I have commanded with the United Nations three times and also with NATO twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you serve in Bosnia in 1994/1995?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went over to Bosnia in April of 1994 and left in May of 1995, for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, while the examination continues, could I please call for ter number 02927, and could I ask - it will be a map - that it be expanded to fill the monitor screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: While we wait for the map to load, General, how did it come about that you were sent to Bosnia the first time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: As part of my Canadian forces, from time to time we are selected to go overseas to fill missions as per Canada's mandate. I was asked to go to Bosnia to become the military assistant to the sector commander of Sarajevo. I was selected, screened, and went over for a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, in your last answer you said that you were the military assistant to the commander of Sector Sarajevo. I'm going to ask you to define two things that you said in that answer; first, military assistant, and second, Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: As the military assistant to the commander, it was my responsibility to run the office for the sector commander, to make sure that his calendar and all of the correspondence was done in accordance with his directions, and also to act as his battle adjutant in the sense of when he went out into the field, I would accompany him to make sure that the visits were done, the coordination with the units on the ground, and also to take notes for any meetings that he attended. And the second part of your question was Sector Sarajevo, the commander. Bosnia at the time was broken down into regions -- into sectors. The sector that -- I worked for two French Generals. First, Andre Soubirou was the first one, and then Herve Gobillard. They were responsible for Sector Sarajevo, which comprised the city and the demilitarised zone just south of Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And day in, day out -- the description that you have given most recently is what you were doing on a day in, day out basis as the military assistant to the commander of Sector Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Correct. It comprised, in the morning, of getting his morning briefings ready, doing the correspondence, reviewing the calendar; then going out with him to visit units. At the end of the day, we would also regularly go and visit the commander of Bosnia at the time. It was General Sir Michael Rose, followed by General Sir Rupert Smith. Again, just going to visit any of the Bosnian authorities, both Muslim and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what rank did you yourself hold during the time that you were in Sarajevo as the military assistant to the commander of Sector Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I was a major at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, now turning to the map that is on the monitor in front of you, a few questions. During your time in Sarajevo, did you become familiar with the geography of the city?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Very familiar, as I visited and toured the region with my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you also become familiar with the location of the front lines or, as they're sometimes referred to, the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And did you use this knowledge day in and day out in performing your professional duties?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Before coming to court today, did you have an opportunity to review the map, the original map, which is now on the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How accurate did you find that map to be in terms of the geography of Sarajevo and its surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I thought the map was a very accurate based on what I recall of the region around the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what did you find as far as the accuracy was concerned of the location of the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I thought the symbols on the map for the Serbian and the Bosnian confrontation lines were most accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask the registrar to expand this map, and I'm going to ask that the city of Sarajevo, which is the brown area just below the centre, be the centre of the expanded map. That will be nicely done. Thank you. And if could blow it up just a little bit more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you to mark some locations on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Before I do that, I'm going to tender the unmarked map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P194, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with the position of Lukovica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Does it appear on the map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: There is a pen attached to the monitor that, if you mark with it, it makes a mark on the monitor. Could you put a box at the location of Lukavica and then label it with the letter L.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Was there a location in Sarajevo that was colloquially referred to as ""Sniper Alley""?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is "Sniper Alley" on the portion of the map that's on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Would you draw a line along "Sniper Alley" and then label it with the SA, for the English words "Sniper Alley".

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Does Mount Igman appear on this map or has it been scrolled off?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It's been scrolled off.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. Does the airport appear on this map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you draw a line around the perimeter of the airport and label it with the letter A, for "airport."

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with an area called Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Does it appear on this map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It's just off the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to that. Are you familiar with an area called Sedrenik or Sharpstone?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Does that appear on this map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you circle the Sedrenik/Sharpstone area and label it with the letter S.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will tender the map as marked into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But could I ask the brigadier, was there anything particular about the topography of "Sniper Alley" that made it especially attractive to snipers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a number of buildings along "Sniper Alley" that made it easy for snipers to get in and hide. And because of the roads and the height, the area principally in the south of the city, south of the river, it was conducive for snipers to actually get into good positions and find targets of opportunity in that particular region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, to follow up on the question asked by Mr. Robinson, when you're talking about the snipers, what party do you think they belonged to? Which side? One side or both sides? Which side of the warring factions did they belong to, according to you? Which side used them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both sides used snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about on "Sniper Alley."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were snipers on both sides on "Sniper Alley," but the predominant number of snipers were on the Serbian side, firing into the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I was just ready to continue, Your Honour. If it please the Court, we anticipate having detailed aerial photographs of the "Sniper Alley" area later in this witness's examination. I believe the next order of business is to get an exhibit number for the map as marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let it be numbered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P195, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And now if I could please ask the registrar to put up the clean map and to pull back a bit so that we can get in the features that the General indicated were off the map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, as the map is now, does the area of Ilidza and Mount Igman appear on the map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Igman is just there and so is Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let's start with Ilidza, please. On this map, could you draw a box at the location of Ilidza and mark it with a capital L -- capital I, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you mark Mount Igman. And since that also starts with I, let's call that MT, for "mountain."

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Lastly, was there a road that went over Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Using this map, can you illustrate for us the route of that road.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And for the record, that will be the line in the lower left-hand corner of the map. Your Honours, as marked, I will tender this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P196, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then lastly, if we could have the clean map back again at about this level. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, I'm now going to ask you to make a mark on the map. I'm not going to ask it be admitted into evidence. Rather, once you have made a mark, I'm going to ask the registrar to note that mark and zoom in close on the spot that you are marking, and then we will introduce that. Did you become familiar with some elevated positions around the city the Sarajevo? And I'll give you some names: Debelo Brdo, Mojmilo, and Zuc.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let's start with Debelo Brdo. On this map, can you show us where Debelo Brdo is?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then I will ask the registrar to zoom in very close on the Debelo Brdo area as you indicate it. That's a bit too close. If we could move back a bit, please. That's great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, this one we are going to try to move into evidence eventually. So, General, could you start by marking on this map the position of the hill called Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Were you aware from your time in Sarajevo which of the warring factions controlled Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you tell us the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The Muslims had their positions just below the pimple called Debelo Brdo. The UN were right on the top of it and the Muslim trenches were just below it. And if I could also say, then, the Serbs were just to the south on a higher piece of ground that looked down onto Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll move the admission -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you please mark this with a DB, for "Debelo Brdo."

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And now I will move it into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would he able to identify the positions held as he just described them?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, I can take him through a number of questions about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The three positions; the Muslims, the UN and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, do you see a dotted blue line on this map? It's really not a line; it's a dotted blue perimeter.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What does that signify?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Where the Muslims were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is that their most forward positions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What about the dotted red perimeter? What does that signify?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That signifies the Serbian positions, and from what I remember, there is only one modification I would make.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you describe that modification, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Can I just show it? Just where the line is, you see the road just below the B?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: From what I remember, I do think the Serbs actually controlled that piece of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if we could mark on this, Your Honours, even though it's already admitted, I would ask the General to make a mark on that road. Is that permissible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't see why not, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Then would you please mark on the exhibit. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please make pauses between questions an answers for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Brigadier, I have to ask you to observe a pause between the question and answer. Mr. Docherty knows that very well. The interpreters are concerned about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I know it very well, Your Honour, and I keep forgetting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, what was on the very top of Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: There was a UN position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Can you go into a bit more detail about what that position was? Who was up there? Who commanded it? How many men? Things like that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: From what I recall, it was an a small platoon commanded by a lieutenant. Probably under 30 men were on top of that hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Moving down the hill, what was the first warring faction that you came to?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Just down below the hill towards the west and the east of the position were the Muslim trenches, and they extended down into the city, down into the north, right down into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And as you continue this imaginary walk down the hill, what is the next warring faction that you came to?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Well, if you went south, you actually walked down a bit of a hill but you were walking uphill, where, in fact, the Serbs had their positions, which was slightly above Debelo Brdo. And you could look over the -- sort of a little bit of a dip in the flat area where it went up into the southern part of that map and up higher, and that's where the Serbs were, all along the ridge line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And do I understand that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And then the Serbs occupied the higher position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They occupied dominating ground over this area. The UN had command of this little pimple, I would call it, which was significant, and the Muslims were just down a little bit below and the Serbs were a little bit higher. But the UN had a key piece of ground in that region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What you said, as you walked down the first position, you would meet the Muslim trenches.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which led me to believe that they might have been -- they might have been at the highest position, but that's not so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. The UN was slightly above the Muslims and the Serbs were slightly above the UN, and they had the more dominating ground of the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, when you say that the Serbs were slightly above the Muslims, that was on a different hill.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And from a military point of view, what was the interrelationship between this different higher hill and Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The Serbs had the better position in the region because they commanded that entire ridge line to the south of the city. Debelo Brdo was just this little pimple which was a significant piece of ground that lay between where the Serbs' position was and the city. And the UN had that and the Muslims had what was left, which was the area just on the east and west of it, which was the best they could get in that particular area. But the Serbs had the dominating vantage point in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And now on this exhibit, if we could please take the marks away, leave the map at the current level of zoom, and then we'll mark it again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this map, as marked, will be admitted as Exhibit P197.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with the position called Zuc, or Zuc, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I am. It's where the television tower was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is the area of Zuc on this map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yeah, it's in the upper left corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you put an X on Zuc, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that's rather a big X. Is Zuc in the centre or is that all Zuc?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And for the record, could the record please indicate that the red dot to the right of the X has been indicated by the witness to be the position of Zuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can the X be deleted, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher, could we please delete the markings and we'll try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you put a letter Z beside that, General.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I move the admission of the map as marked, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P198, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, again, if the marks could be taken away. This is the last map marking we're going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with an elevation called Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Does it appear on this map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please pull back on the zoom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Does Mojmilo now appear on this map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Could you please mark its position with a dot and mark it with the letter M.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I move the admission of this map as marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P199, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. We're finished with map marking and SMART Boards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, the two elevations we were just talking about, Zuc and then Mojmilo, let's start with Zuc. Who controlled Zuc, which warring faction?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Top to bottom?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And the same question with regard to Mojmilo. Who controlled Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And again, top to bottom?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move now to a different topic and that's the topic of sniping. Were sniping attacks on civilians a concern during the time that you were in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, how it was that the United Nations troops in the city would learn about sniping attacks on civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We would learn a number of different ways, either from our forces who were on the ground as part of the anti-sniping task force or in the form of protests from one of the warring factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: These protests from the warring factions, what form did they take? Telephone, face-to-face, letters, what have you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: They could take the form of telephone, of face-to-face meetings, or letters. In all cases they were investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What did that investigation consist of? Once a report came in, what did the UN do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: What we would do is take the particulars of the protest, apply it to the applicable battalion that was in the area, go find out as much detail as we could, including from the local authorities, and then reply to the protest from that specific warring faction. In many cases, it would also generate further communications and discussions with the warring factions, especially the ones who did the action, to tell them to don't -- to cease this type of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, in general, how effective were these discussions with the warring faction that the UN concluded lay behind the particular incident that was being investigated?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: What would normally happen is that we would have an increase in sniping incidents, which would be characterised by multiple meetings. It would generate into a significant series of discussions and get to a point where, in fact, we would be engaging at the corps commander level with the sector commander, or in fact the commander of Bosnia at the time, either Michael Rose or Rupert Smith. And after a significant intervention by my boss, the sector commander, or the commander of Bosnia, the situation would get better for a while, but then would be a slow, gradual build-up of these incidents until we got to another stage where we'd have to make more concerted efforts to curtail sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, it's time for the break. We'll take the adjournment for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We should congratulate ourselves. We did 18 minutes instead of 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, for literally no more than three minutes. Way off my stride this morning and I omitted to have the last photograph marked by the last witness tendered as an exhibit, and I would like to do that now, if you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P200, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, just before the break you were talking about the pattern you typically observed when a protest was made to one or the other of the warring factions. From those observations, can you draw any conclusions as to the effectiveness of command and control over the activities being protested about; and, if so, what are those conclusions and what are the reasons for them?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: From my observation, it appeared that there was a commander's intent in play around the city of Sarajevo with respect to sniping incidents, illustrated by the fact that we had sniping along "Sniper Alley", we had sniping around the airport, and we had sniping around the Sharpstone area, which -- three separate areas, three separate organisations, which would indicate to me, based on my military experience, of a higher commander's intent at play here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want now, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, as did you in relation to "Sniper Alley," whether the other two locations had sniping from both sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall from up in the Sharpstone area that most of the sniping came from the Serbian side. "Sniper Alley," it was predominantly from the Serbian side, and the airport area, I think it was about equal. Maybe a little bit more from the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, then, in relation to the Sharpstone area, you said most came from the Serbian side, which I take to mean that some did come from the other side, and -- well, "Sniper Alley," you say, was predominantly from the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, I want to take up some of these positions in turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to start with "Sniper Alley," and I'm going to ask the court registrar to call up ter number 2819, an aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, General, are you familiar with an area of Sarajevo called Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: May I ask the registrar, is it possible to resize the photograph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, looking at this photograph, do you see on it the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What colour is the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It is a yellowish colour at the top centre of the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Is there a road in front of the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, there is, commonly referred to as "Sniper Alley."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And down at the -- about the middle of picture, do you see a line of trees on a left-right orientation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, and that would be delineate where the river, the Miljacka river, was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And did the Miljacka river have any military significance at the time that you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It delineated the division between the Muslims and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: At the bottom of the photograph, there is what appears to me to be a dense residential area. Can you tell us which of the warring factions controlled that area at the bottom of the screen?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the neighbourhood that you have just indicated was controlled by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I do believe -- I believe it was called the Grbavica area, but I'd have to see a bigger map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And now if we could please see ter number 02930, also an aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, on the monitor in front of you is an aerial photograph. Do you recognise the scene that's depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Does the road that you have referred to as "Sniper Alley" appear in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It's not clear, but I know it's just on the other side of the -- of those big tall buildings. You can see there the trees that delineate the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And could you help us out by using the pen and just drawing a line along the Miljacka river, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I will be asking for another mark but not for five or ten questions, however you want to handle it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, is the area known as Grbavica in this photograph that is on the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I think it's just off to the top right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, along "Sniper Alley," did you yourself ever see a Serbian sniper nest?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: My boss and I visited one at one stage when we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can you tell us the approximate date of this visit?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It would have been in the spring or summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can you tell us how this visit came about?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We had been concerned with sniping throughout the time that we were there. We had heard about a number of positions, and we had -- we had asked the Serbians if we could actually go and visit some of the buildings and they escorted us to one of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is the building to which you were escorted on the photograph on the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you please put an X through the building that you visited.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Can we just zoom in; is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could we take the markings away, please, Mr. Registrar, and then zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Does that help, General?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, before you mark the building, to remark the river.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And now could you put an X on the building.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I move the admission of the photograph as marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P201, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, that concludes my marking for the foreseeable future.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, when you went into that building, what did you see that was significant to you in terms of whether that building had ever been used by snipers?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It was a three- to four-storey red brick building. We walked up a number of stairs, and as we walked through the building we noticed that there were holes punched through the wall. Some people would call those a spider hole. But you could actually look out towards the Muslim side of the river. There were sandbags that could be used as positions for shooters and other paraphernalia that could be used for shooters throughout the building that snipers could utilise in the prosecution of their task.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And from those observations that you've just described, did you draw any conclusions, as a military officer, about the uses to which this red building in Grbavica had been put?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It was a good position for snipers, and from my experience it definitely looked like it was prepared for that use.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did sniping occur along the whole length -- excuse me. Earlier today you marked on the map "Sniper Alley." Did sniping occur the whole length of the line that you drew on that map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you, during your time in Sarajevo, come into possession of information about sniper nests elsewhere in the city, other than the red building that you have drawn an X through on the exhibit in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We had information of a number of buildings and positions throughout the city, principally along "Sniper Alley," where in fact actions had taken place. This was extensively mapped out by the anti-sniping task force that was positioned every day along "Sniper Alley," led by the French, supported by the Ukrainians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to get to the anti-sniping task force in just a couple of minutes. But before I do that, a couple of questions on a different topic. Were you aware of allegations that the Bosnian Muslim side had engaged in shooting its own civilians in order to generate press that would be favourable to their side anti the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I was aware of, in fact, two incidents and also a third shelling incident that was precipitated by the Serbs but finished off by the Bosnians, the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, when you make that statement about two incidents plus the shelling incident, could we take those up in turn, please, and in whatever order makes the most sense for you. Just pick one incident, describe it, then the next, and then the third.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The first one was, the French were in possession of a video showing a Muslim sniper shooting his own people. I never saw the video. I heard about it from the French officers in my office and from my French boss. And it was referred to with the Muslim vice-president in one meeting we had when he was trying to accuse the other side, the Serbs, of doing something, when, in fact, we knew that he was culpable, which was associated with the shelling incident I talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in regards to that, let's turn to the shelling incident, since they seem to lead into each other. What was the date of the shelling incident that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The shelling incident took place, I believe, around the 18th/19th of September. It started off with two mortar attacks in the span of about 40 minutes. The first attack hit the city, and about, as I say, about 40 minutes later, another mortar attack hit the same spot. And what normally happens after these attacks, you do get a congregation of people and there were twice the number of casualties. We, as a result of that, as a result of all the shelling attacks in the city, put together an investigating team, in this particular case led by Lieutenant Colonel Lechevallier, a French officer. It was a joint investigation with the Muslim authorities, being, in this case, the Muslim police. The Muslim police actually gave us the 82-millimetre mortar firing tables which we used. When we conducted the investigation, the crater analysis, we actually found out that the shells came from two different directions. Because of the sensitivity of our findings, we tried to contact the Muslim authorities to indicate to them that, in fact, they were culpable because the second rounds actually came parallel to the river on the Muslim side, when the first rounds came across the river from the Serbian positions. The Muslims didn't want to talk to us initially, so we had the press conference and my boss talked about how we were going to issue out the press conference, and said we would not make conclusions. We would explain to the public how we conducted our analysis, lay the facts on the table, tell them who was part of the investigating team, and let the people make their own conclusions. It was pretty obvious at the end that everyone said the first rounds came from the Serbian side, which we -- we just let them make their own conclusions, and the second rounds came from the Muslim side, at which point we were immediately summoned to the vice-president who was downtown. He brought into the meeting the media and everyone else, at which point we said the Muslims were part of the investigating team, and that we also had evidence that this was not the first time; that there was also a tape that was in the possession of the French, at which point the vice-president dismissed everybody out of the room and it was just my boss, a few French officers and myself and the vice-president there. And it became a little bit more humble, not quite as much rhetoric; when, in fact, he knew then that we had the information and it was not a bluff, and he became a little bit more submissive at that stage in the game.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That was a very long answer. Exceptionally, I allowed it, but, as you know, my predilection is for short answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just to pick up on a couple of the points that you just spoke about, General. You yourself never did see the tape that your boss possessed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did your boss - that would be General Soubirou - confirm to you ever that such a tape existed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And do you know anything about the date of the incident that allegedly is caught on this tape?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Turning now -- you mentioned that -- you talked about one sniping and one shelling incident. Am I correct that there was one other incident that you wanted to discuss in connection with this issue?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: There was a third incident where, in fact, some French soldiers related to us that they had come across some Muslims filming a staged attack with children - no one was actually hurt; it was all staged - that they were preparing to use on the TV against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Now, circling back to the Bosnian Serb snipers along "Sniper Alley" that you have talked about, you mentioned in your testimony before -- just after the break that you had drawn certain conclusions about the level at which these snipers were controlled. Who was the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps during the 13 months that you were in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: There were two Serbian commanders when I was there. The first one was General Galic and then the second one was General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you ever meet General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I met him several times with my boss. Numerous times.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximate date for the first time that you met General Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I believe the first time I met him would have been sometime around the May/June period of the summer of 1994 when I first got there, going around with General Soubirou, touring the battle space, and dealing with the commanders on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you meet General Dragomir Milosevic often enough to form an opinion of him as a military officer?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I did. And during the meetings that we had, he appeared competent as a commander, but at the same time he appeared somewhat troubled by what he was doing. And notwithstanding that, he did appear to have a lot of influence from Indic, who was an LO, who really spoke to the Serbian higher headquarters in Pale. And on some occasions, General Milosevic tried to deal with us and leave Indic out of it, which -- again, trying to work with and accommodate the UN on some of the issues that he was facing, principally around Sierra 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You said Indic and then you used the abbreviation LO. What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Indic was a major at the time. I think he was promoted colonel by -- lieutenant colonel by the time I left. He was a liaison officer from Pale, and he really did speak on behalf of the Serbian higher command to make sure that what they were doing was being executed at the lowest level -- at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You indicated in an answer a few minutes ago that at times General Milosevic appeared, in your words, "troubled" by the things that he was asked to do. Did you ever have a conversation with General Milosevic in which he elaborated on any personal consequences to himself about the things that he was doing in Sarajevo during 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: (redacted) I asked him at that stage - and, again, I believe it was him - whether or not he was ever going to visit his daughter, and he told me that he would never be able to leave Bosnia because of what he was doing in the country and how it was going to be perceived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Was there discussions between yourself and Dragomir Milosevic concerning a checkpoint called Sierra 4?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, my boss and General Milosevic had discussions about Sierra 4, which was just outside of the airport on route to the PTT building. It was an area of contention with the UN, that our freedom of movement was severely hampered by the Serbs there. General Milosevic had an agreement with my boss to improve the circulation of that area. He did this through the Ilidza Brigade, I believe it was, and we kept Indic out of it which we knew was going to irritate the Serbian higher command, but it was designed to, A, improve our freedom of movement, as we were exercising our right, and did demonstrate the General's attempt to at least try to work with us, at least at that particular point in time, a little bit more amenable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, from these discussions over the Sierra 4 checkpoint and from the role that Dragomir Milosevic played in these discussions, were you able to draw any conclusions as to the control over the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps exercised by Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: From my observation and dealings with him, he did have command and control over the corps and over operations around the city. When we went to him with concerns about sniping, the situation would normally afterwards get a little bit better for a while, and then we would have to re-engage with him when situations were getting a little bit more tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to follow up on the question of control over the snipers and anti-sniping efforts in just a minute. But before I do that, you testified earlier that in your career you've commanded military formations that include snipers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: From those experiences, are you able to draw any conclusions about the quality of sniper units by observing the way in which they work?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Snipers -- yes. Snipers are a highly specialised skill set that is normally commanded at the higher levels. As a battalion commander, I would control the snipers; as a brigade commander, I would control how we would employ snipers because of the paucity of numbers; but more importantly is the effect that you're looking for in the application of this skill set. It's very precise, and you want to make sure you apply them to very precise targets that you're looking for. The snipers that I saw operating in Sarajevo were very competent, based upon comments I received from the anti-sniping task force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you talk about snipers engaged by the anti-sniping task force, the anti-sniping task force engaged snipers of which warring faction?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The ones down along "Sniper Alley" were mainly focused against the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: With regard to the anti-sniping efforts, could I please ask the registrar to call up 65 ter number 1917. And it's the left-hand document on the split screen that I want to ask General Fraser about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. I regret, we don't seem to have a B/C/S translation, so I'll just ask a couple of -- I'll just ask you what it is.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This is an order to the anti- -- in fact, it's an order to all the battalions for anti-sniping measures for Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And who is this order coming from and who is this order going to?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This order came from the headquarters under the authority of the commander. It's signed off by the senior operations officer, Lieutenant Colonel Peter Anthony, who was a French marine. This is the way that the French conducted business. Everything that was directed by the commander would be followed up by orders, fragmentary orders, and this one is specifically designed for anti-sniping measures around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I move into evidence 65 ter number 1917, the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P202, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Brigadier, can you just clarify for me how the anti-sniper unit was intended to carry out its work? I'm looking here at the execution, although it's not very visible, and I see "Deterrence." It's a little clearer now. Deterrence was one part of the strategy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was. For the force just to be physically out there, to deter both sides, principally, though, the Serbs, from shooting at civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And how would they do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By physically interposing themselves between the Serbian side and the civilians. For example, along "Sniper Alley," we would physically have vehicles and UN soldiers along that alley at the principal points where, in fact, snipers would be engaging civilians, and we'd put ourselves between them and the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So was that successful, the mere physical presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To some degree. We also put up passive barriers. But even the physical presence of those soldiers wasn't all that good, because at one stage we had a -- one stage I remember, we had a French soldier shot in the head from a Serbian sniper. I -- actually, we both went down there and watched the soldier taken away in an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, let's go back to the document we see on the screen. First paragraph, "Situation." You said yourself that you had led units in which there were snipers or sniper formations. I imagine that this is part of regular activities within the armed forces, having snipers. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at the first paragraph of this document. This document reads that the activities of snipers from both sides were increasing at the time. Here is my question: From both sides snipers were shooting at each other, or does that mean that from both sides snipers would shoot civilians and possibly would fire on their own population? Because it can be interpreted in different ways. Here, what is said is that Serbs could shoot on other Serbs, or it could also mean that Muslims, Muslim troops, could have shot on other Muslims. From that paragraph this can be inferred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The intent of this order was to stop Serbs, principally, and Muslims from firing on civilians. The employment of snipers is designed to employ legitimate military targets. If Serbs were firing against Muslim soldiers, like soldier to soldier, we in the UN did not intervene into those operations. That was a -- legitimate military targets doing what they were doing. Where we intervened, and where this order was designed to intervene, was from snipers engaging in civilians who were not deemed combatants in this conflict. We were there to protect the people and do whatever measures we needed to go after those individuals who were attacking civilians, not soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand this, of course. But I would like to know, whether unintentionally or voluntarily, Serb soldiers fired against Serb civilians, and if -- on the other side if, intentionally or unintentionally, Muslim soldiers shot at Muslim civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of Serbs firing at Serb civilians, and I only have the one case where I was told about a Muslim sniper firing at Muslim civilians and then the shelling incident. Those are the only two examples I have of that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order not to waste too much time, I think there is a need for a redaction in the transcript, the place where our client lives. I did not realise, but maybe this element of information should remain within the walls of this courtroom. I don't think it is necessary to reveal the exact location where the daughter lives. It was some 15 minutes ago, I believe. Maybe we can go over the transcript very quickly, because I know there's a 30-minute lag between what is said in the courtroom and the broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has decided that the reference will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I have that at page 85, line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I was asking a little bit ago, General, about your evaluation of the quality of these snipers. You indicated that you had received stories back from the anti-sniping units that we've just been talking about. Tell us, please, what stories you were hearing back from the anti-sniping units and what role those stories played in you evaluating the quality of the Bosnian Serbian snipers.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The French soldiers would report back, and I talked to some about the quality, and they indicated to me they were very competent at what they were doing. For example, at "Sniper Alley," soldiers would regularly hear the incoming Serbian snipers come in, that they would fire at a telephone pole to tell -- indicate to them they were there. Following that, it was not uncommon for the snipers to register their positions by firing a couple of shots to check on windage and distance and to set themselves up for the day's activities. And then at the end of the day, from time to time it was not uncommon for a sniper to pop off a -- to fire a round off the side of one of our vehicles to say that he was leaving for the day. It was an unwritten code, if I may say that, between the snipers and the UN anti-sniping task force, and it was also indicating, "I'm here. Try to find me." And we had a lot of troops down there and it was hard to find these people. They were good.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How good were the anti-sniping teams? What sort of soldiers were on those anti-sniping teams?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The corps of the anti-sniping team was the French -- the French battalion at the airport, the French battalion along "Sniper Alley." And we had also special reconnaissance and special troops assigned to them. They were designed to go and find the snipers, and they had a hard time finding them. But when they did find them, we would engage snipers. And if we received a vociferous response back from one of the warring factions, we had a pretty good indication that we had gotten one of their snipers. If we didn't hear anything back, we didn't get anybody. So yelling meant good.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did any of these French soldiers lose their lives during these anti-sniping operations?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We had one soldier, as I indicated to you before, who was shot and wounded on "Sniper Alley." We had a second soldier who was moving a passive -- a C can. He was an a fork-lift operator. He was shot in the vehicle. He actually fell out of the vehicle and he died on TV. In fact, that's how his wife found out that he had died; she watched him die on TV. We only found out in the headquarters about 15 minutes later. And the third one was we had a soldier on the seventeenth floor, I believe, in the Unis tower, looking through a sighting system, and he was shot right through the sighting system and shot into the head. He subsequently died of his wounds, and that was a very, very hard shot to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just explain to us what that means. He is looking through the sighting system, which is a hole the circumference of which would be, what, or the diameter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This French soldier was looking through what was called a Milan anti-tank sighting system. It wasn't being used for any tank. It was a system that actually magnified, so it was about -- a sight about probably 10 -- well, the mechanism he was looking for was probably about 10 inches in circumference. Back in a room, looking down "Sniper Alley," and some sniper on the other side found him in a window and shot him, and it must have been well over 300, 400 metres, a long shot, to get him to shoot through that sighting system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that would call for great skill.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a very, very difficult shot, and I do recall that we were very, very surprised that we lost a soldier in that particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And did the anti-sniping unit take out any of the snipers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the numbers. I know that we were effective along "Sniper Alley" and we were also effective in the airport and I know we did fire back at Sharpstone, Sedrenik. We were actually looking for, in fact, a woman up there that was allegedly sniping against the Muslims who supposedly was of Olympic quality. That was one of the individuals we were looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, just to follow up on that. Having taken out some of the snipers, would you then have been able to determine their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could not determine their ethnicity. We could tell you from what side of the confrontation line it was fired from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
