utterances.text: Yes. Put it that way, then. Answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we could tell from which side they were firing at. To answer you and further explain, I think it was around the -- in April of 1995, a French soldier was coming back from the airport. He was shot and killed coming through the airport, and another French soldier was shot and killed by a sniper along "Sniper Alley." One of those snipers was a Serbian that we determined along "Sniper Alley"; the other one we determined -- we ascertained was probably a Muslim sniper, and that one was at the airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, a couple of minutes ago there was a question from, I believe, Judge Mindua concerning paragraph 1 of the document that is in front of you, and I believe that the question indicated -- keyed off the use of the phrase "snipers from both sides." Were Serbian civilians still living in Grbavica at the time when you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And were there also Serbian military targets in the Grbavica area of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Consisting of?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It would have been brigade line troops that were manning the line down there, plus snipers. Both sides manned lines throughout the city that was interspersed with civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I think you came close to answering this question in response to a slightly different question from the Bench, but to be sure, can you describe to us briefly what is the proper military use of a sniper.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Snipers are typically used for high-value military targets, be that military commanders, radio operators, but not, in any of my experience/training, civilians. They do not constitute targets. And snipers also are very good, and it's not normally possible to miss who you're looking for, as a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, I believe your question was regarding an individual person. What about the situation of a tram, particularly a tram that is articulated in the middle? Would you expect a sniper of the quality you have been describing on the Bosnian Serb side along "Sniper Alley" to hit a tram by mistake? And after you have answered the question, could you give us your reasons for the answer.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It's unlikely that you could miss and hit a tram. From my experience, trams were a favourite target of snipers inside of Sarajevo because of the psychological impact it had on the people of Sarajevo. The people looked to the tram, and if it was running, things were reasonably good; if it was stopped, it meant that the situation was grave and that sent shudders throughout the city. So shooting at a tram had a significant psychological impact on the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then lastly on the question of sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If I could please ask the registrar to pull up ter number 2009 and I'll be interested in e-court pages 2 and 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document, General, did the anti-sniping teams write reports about the activities in which they had been engaged?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: All the time. And I will say, the French were meticulous at writing reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you now is e-court page 2 of ter number 2009. Is this a document that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It appears to be a -- yes, I do recognise this. It appears to be a log and from -- who it's coming from, RusBat, FreBat. It appears to have come from the headquarters in the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Why do you think it has come from the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Because we're talking about the Russian Battalion, FreBat 2, a liaison officer from the Serbian side. All those individuals would have reported up through the headquarters, the sector headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And could I ask the registrar to please go to e-court page 7 of this ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the type of document that is now on the screen in front of you, General?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What kind of a document is this?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This would be a typical summary of incidents that would happen that we would produce for not only the commander but for other people, including our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I move the admission into evidence of 65 ter number 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, I want to turn now to the topic of mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just before you leave that. May I ask the brigadier, a sniper aiming at a moving tram - and I realise this probably begs the question - would have been aiming at the tram generally rather than any particular individual, any particular passenger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most snipers would probably try to pick out a target inside that tram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Even though the tram is moving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They're taught how to shoot moving targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, you've testified that on two occasions in your career you have commanded -- I don't remember if it was a mortar platoon or a mortar company. But based on your training and experience, are you able to watch the effects of a mortar crew's work and tell how good that mortar crew is?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Based on my two command times, commanding a mortar platoon, I can just a competent mortar crew, and the mortar crews that I saw in Sarajevo were competent. They could hit, generally, the area they were looking at firing at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Was the Serbian fire onto the city of Sarajevo ever, in your opinion, responding to fire onto the Serbs by the defenders of the city?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Sometimes when the Muslims would fire out, the Serbians, in general, would fire back, and normally when that happened the Serbs would always fire back. A lot more came back than went out. And in one particular case, the Muslims actually fired at the Lukavica corps headquarters, which was completely against the convention when I was there. Neither corps headquarters was attacked. And the result of the Muslims firing against the Serbian corps headquarters was a huge barrage coming back at the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you say coming back at the city, did this barrage come on to the source of fire at Lukavica? Did it go elsewhere? Could you elaborate, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The return fire did not go back to where the origin was. It was just fired at the city. In fact, it was firing around Debelo Brdo and the area just around Miljacka river, on the Muslim side. But it was -- it was intense.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In your time with the Canadian army, have you become familiar with a term of art, proportionality of response? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can you summarise for the Judges the training that you have had to help you under the concept, proportionality of response?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It is a foundation of the training that any Canadian soldier receives, which includes rules of engagement, military justified, proportionality, and collateral damage. It is a key aspect of how we apply force in the Canadian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: As a result of the training that you have had which you described as a core feature of being a Canadian soldier, could you describe the hallmarks or the criteria of what you would consider to be a proportional response or, to put the question a little differently, without giving us the answer, tell us how you would go about analysing the question, was a response proportionate?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We would go through an estimate process of determining the military necessity of returning fire, what type of fire we were -- actually had received to begin with, and normally you try to return fire with the same type of fire and minimise the effects to collateral, being people, places or things. And let me give you an example. If a sniper shot at me, I would try to fire back with a sniper. Precise with precise. And try not to overuse the force that I have in the effect that I want to deliver at the other end.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want you now to apply those criteria or that method of analysing the question of proportionality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, before listening to the question I believe that is going in the direction which is a bit -- we're looking at facts only. We're busy without a job because we're looking at -- you were supposed to look at facts, and I think that the direction that we're taking right now is going to leave you without a job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but one of the issues that the Chamber will have to determine is proportionality and the whole question of excessive force, and this is a witness who has had practical experience in the field. I think his evidence can only be helpful, and I have already identified the limits of questioning of this kind, and as far as I can see, Mr. Docherty is keeping within those limits. The evidence so far from the witness is that you return sniper with sniper, precise with precise, and mortar with mortar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But again, further complicated by the fact that -- for example, we could not return fire at the airport. At the east end of the airport where the Serbian position was that would fire on to the airport, we could not return fire because we did not have precise -- enough -- a weapons system that was precise enough to get out to that range without causing potential collateral damage to the civilians who were around the firing unit that fired back at us. So, again, we identified the target that we had to shoot back. It was a military necessity. It was proportional we could use a weapon system, but we didn't have a weapons system that had enough precision that could ensure mitigating potential collateral damage to the people who lived around that firing unit. So that -- in that case, we did not return fire. So like with like. Proportionate, define military necessity, but we couldn't establish collateral damage. It was too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Your Honour, please, I have one thing to add with the interpretation. I'm really sorry, I know that it's a difficult job, just like ours. But here what I've told you is not what I meant. It was a bit -- I would never dare say this. I think the interpreter went a bit too far. I would never have talked to you in this way. So I really apologise. I -- this is not reflecting what I said. This is not what I meant -- it's what I meant but I wouldn't have said it this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General, could you please use the methodology that you have just been describing to us and apply it to the Bosnian Serb response to the Bosnian Muslim attack on the Lukavica Barracks that you were just talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, there now, Mr. Docherty, you are going to be asking him whether a particular situation -- in a particular situation the response was proportional.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I thought, and I apologise if I'm wrong, but I thought from the discussion with the Witness Nicolai that having gone through the preceding questions that that question was allowed by the Chamber. If I am mistaken in that, I will withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I'll do now is I'll take the break and we'll ruminate on it.
